name: Safravi
tagline: Sharp mind, quick fire, and a to-do list that actually gets done.
share_line: I spark fast, forgive fast, and finish first.

free.summary:
In Unani tradition, Fire (Safravi) is the mizaj of safra, yellow bile, the warm and dry humour linked with fire and summer. If you are Fire, you move through life like a lit matchstick: bright, quick and purposeful. You are the one who submits the assignment two days early, books the family holiday while everyone else is still debating dates in the group chat, and spots the single typo in a 40-slide presentation.

People admire your drive and sometimes fear your tongue. You have little patience for slow decisions, vague answers or rush-hour traffic. Your anger can flare in seconds, but it usually burns out just as fast, and you rarely carry it for long.

Physically, Unani texts picture the Fire person as lean, active and warm, with a sharp appetite, quick digestion and a strong dislike of heat. Many Fire people find they feel calmest and most focused with cool, moist foods, regular meals and enough sleep, especially through a long, hot summer, wherever you spend it.
traits: Driven and decisive; you would rather make a call than sit in uncertainty.
A sharp, analytical mind that spots flaws, shortcuts and solutions quickly.
A direct speaker: you say what you think, sometimes before checking the tone.
A natural leader in a crunch, from exam week to organising a mehndi in three days.
A temper that flares fast and cools fast; long grudges are rarely your style.
Competitive and proud of your standards; 'good enough' rarely feels good enough.
body_signs: Unani texts describe a lean, wiry or athletic build that doesn't gain weight easily.
Skin tends to feel warm and dry, and you may flush quickly in heat or anger.
Sharp hunger: skipping a meal can make you irritable fast, the classic 'hangry'.
Strong thirst, and chilli or oily food can bring on a burning 'garmi' feeling.
Lighter sleep than most; a busy mind can keep you awake past midnight.
Hot weather and stuffy, overheated rooms drain you quickly, while cool air feels like relief.
free.quick_tip: Never let yourself get too hungry. Keep a cooling snack close by, such as cucumber, a few soaked almonds or a glass of lassi. Unani tradition suggests a Fire temper rises fastest on an empty, overheated stomach.

premium.deep_dive:
In the Canon, Ibn Sina described safra as the sharpest and lightest of the four humours: hot, dry and quick to move. It was believed to give the body its digestive fire and the mind its edge. A Fire (Safravi) person, in this picture, is someone in whom that fire burns a little brighter than average. It is a gift for getting things done, and it needs cooling to stay a gift.

In the body, Unani tradition associates this mizaj with a lean, firm frame, warm and dry skin, quick digestion and strong thirst. Heat is your weak point. Hot afternoons, chilli-heavy curries, back-to-back chai or coffee and late nights are all traditionally believed to add fuel to an already strong fire. When the balance tips, many Fire people notice irritability, a hot or burning feeling after meals, restless sleep and a very short fuse. The traditional response is cooling and moistening: water, fresh fruit, gourds, sensible amounts of dairy, and rest.

In the mind, the fire gives clarity and speed. You can see the end of a project before others have read the brief, and you are often the family member who handles the bank, the visa forms, the property papers or the hospital admission, because you will get it done. The risk is impatience. You may finish other people's sentences, skip the feelings part of a conversation, or treat a relaxed spouse as a problem to be solved.

Emotionally, Fire people are traditionally described as brave, ambitious and proud, with anger close to the surface but not deep beneath it. You rarely sulk; you erupt and move on, sometimes before the other person has recovered. Learning to pause, cool down and repair is your lifelong practice.

Across life stages, Unani tradition saw the prime years, roughly the twenties and thirties, as naturally warm and dry, so a young Fire person may feel all fire: competitive, restless, impatient with elders. As the body is traditionally believed to cool with age, many Fire people mellow in their forties and fifties into the calm, wise problem-solver of the family.

Across the seasons, summer is both your mirror and your challenge. The tradition linked safra with hot, dry weather, so the hottest months can feel brutal, whether you spend them in the Gulf or in a city flat built to trap heat. Rain brings some relief, and winter is usually when you feel most balanced, clear-headed and kind. Living well as a Fire person means respecting your fire: using it for your work, and cooling it before it reaches your words.

foods_favour.why: Cool and moist by Unani reckoning; the classic gentle vegetable for a warm, dry mizaj.
Cooling and hydrating; a plate beside every summer meal is a simple Fire habit.
Cool and moist; traditionally eaten between meals in summer to settle heat and thirst.
Cool and moist; a bowl of raita beside spicy food softens its heat.

foods_favour.item: Milk, plain or with soaked almonds
foods_favour.why: Traditionally considered cool and moist, calming for an overheated, restless system.
A classic Unani choice for calming safra; sweet-sour, cooling and refreshing.
Classical texts name tamarind as a calmer of safra; enjoy it in sharbat or chutney.
Cooling and moistening when sweet; traditionally used for heat and thirst.
Light, cool-leaning and easy on digestion, ideal on hot or stressful days.
Gourds and squash are traditionally cool and moist, keeping meals light and soothing.
Both traditionally cool; Unani texts value lettuce for calming a busy, heated mind.
Soaking softens their warmth; tradition values them for moisture and a steadier mind.
Sour-sweet and cooling by Unani reasoning; easy supermarket answers to summer heat.

foods_favour.item: Barley in soup, or barley flour in roti
foods_favour.why: Cool by Unani reckoning and gentle, a good weekday swap for heavy parathas.

foods_limit.item: Red chilli and heavy garam masala
foods_limit.why: Strongly hot and dry; tradition sees them as fuel for an already blazing fire.
Chilli, oil and smoke together; enjoy occasionally with raita and salad, not every week.

foods_limit.item: Fried snacks like pakoras, samosas and crisps
foods_limit.why: Hot oil adds heat and dryness and can leave you irritable and thirsty.

foods_limit.item: Cup after cup of chai and coffee
foods_limit.why: Both are traditionally hot and dry; five cups a day is a classic Fire trap.
Pickles and salt add heat and dryness; a spoonful on the side is plenty.
Warm by tradition; one or two after a meal, not a summer-long mango marathon.

foods_limit.item: Garlic and ginger by the handful
foods_limit.why: Strongly hot and dry; keep them as flavouring, not as the main event.
Unani rates honey hot and dry; a teaspoon is fine, spoonfuls are not.

foods_limit.item: Walnuts, pistachios and dry fruit in summer
foods_limit.why: Warm and drying; save larger portions for the cooler winter months.
Stimulating and dehydrating; they feed restlessness rather than cooling it.

drinks: Lassi, sweet or salted: cool and moist, the classic summer calmer for Fire
Imli sharbat with little sugar: sour-sweet and traditionally used to settle safra
Coconut water: cooling and hydrating on long, hot afternoons
Basil seeds (sabja) soaked in lemon water: traditionally cooling and hydrating
Rose sharbat with less sugar: cooling and calming on summer evenings
Cold milk blended with soaked almonds and cardamom: a simple cooler that helps you unwind at night
spices_herbs: Dhania (coriander seeds and leaves): traditionally cool, a gentle everyday base
Saunf (fennel): chewed after meals, many people find it freshens and settles
Elaichi (green cardamom): fragrant and light, a calmer alternative to strong masala chai
Rose water: a few drops in milk, lassi or kheer, traditionally cooling and calming
Fresh pudina in chutney or raita: refreshing beside spicy food, in small amounts
Go easy on red chilli, black pepper and dried ginger: keep heat as seasoning, never the main event

daily_routine.morning: Wake early and move before the day heats up: a walk, a swim or some stretching around sunrise. Don't charge into the day on chai or coffee alone. Have a cooling, steady breakfast such as a roti with yogurt, an egg, soaked almonds or porridge oats with milk. Before opening your inbox or the family group chat, take two minutes to plan the day calmly.
daily_routine.midday: Eat lunch on time; a late lunch is when your temper peaks. Choose dal, sabzi, raita and salad over spicy takeaway. Step out of the sun or the stuffy office, sip water steadily rather than gulping it all at once, and take a five-minute pause between back-to-back meetings or lectures.
daily_routine.evening: Use the evening for something that cools rather than competes: a walk after sunset, time with family, or a hobby with no deadline. Keep dinner light and mildly spiced, ideally by 8 pm. Leave politics, office complaints and heated debates away from the dinner table.
daily_routine.sleep: Your mind races at night, so build a wind-down. Switch off screens 30 to 45 minutes before bed, keep the room cool and dark, and try a glass of cool milk with cardamom. Aim for seven to eight hours. Writing tomorrow's to-do list before bed stops it looping in your head.

seasons.summer: Your toughest season. Tradition says safra peaks with the heat, so expect a shorter fuse and stronger thirst, whether it's a Gulf summer or a city heatwave in a home without air conditioning. Drink water, lassi and coconut water through the day, eat gourds, cucumber and watermelon, and cut down on chilli, fried food and chai. Exercise only early morning or late evening.
seasons.rains: Rain brings relief, but humid weeks can unsettle digestion. Eat freshly cooked, mildly spiced food and skip anything left sitting out. If you live somewhere grey and drizzly much of the year, cool, damp air often suits Fire: enjoy a walk in the rain, then one chai, not four.
seasons.winter: Usually your happiest season: cool air balances your inner heat, and many Fire people feel clearer and kinder now. Enjoy nuts, carrots, eggs and the occasional halwa. In a long, cold winter, central heating and dry indoor air can parch your skin and lips, so keep drinking water and open a window now and then.
seasons.spring: Spring warms things up and, for many families, brings weddings and festivals: late nights, rich food and family politics. Pace yourself between functions, choose raita and salad at buffets, and protect your sleep. Hold your opinions on the seating plan until you have eaten.

premium.movement: You have natural energy and a competitive streak, so you'll enjoy sports with a score: badminton, squash, cricket, football or running. Balance them with cooling, calming movement such as swimming, gentle stretching or long evening walks. Unani tradition cautions a warm, dry mizaj against exhausting exercise in the heat, so skip midday workouts in summer and overheated gyms. Stop before you are drained; for you, 'one more set' is often the one that leaves you irritable for the rest of the day.
premium.emotional_balance: Unani counts the emotions (harkat-o-sukoon-e-nafsani) among the six essential factors of health, and anger is the emotion tradition links most closely with safra. Your feelings move fast: you feel slighted, react, and are done in five minutes, while the other person is still hurting. Practise a pause: leave the room, drink a glass of water, splash cool water on your face, then come back to the conversation. Learn to say 'let me think about it' instead of delivering an instant verdict. Make time for activities you are not trying to win. If irritability, anxiety or sleeplessness persist for weeks, speak to a doctor or counsellor; that is strength, not weakness.
premium.fasting: Long fasts in hot weather are hardest on a Fire body, whether you keep Ramadan, a vrat, a weekly fast or an intermittent-fasting window. Before the fast, eat slowly and include yogurt, an egg, roti or oats, cucumber and two or three glasses of water spread out. Skip salty, spicy food that leaves you thirsty by noon. Break the fast with water and lassi or fruit, then a light, mildly spiced meal. Expect a shorter temper near the end, and save hard conversations for afterwards.

when_out_of_balance: Snapping at family over small things, then feeling guilty an hour later.
Feeling hot, thirsty and restless even when everyone else is comfortable.
Lying awake replaying conversations or running tomorrow's to-do list.
A burning 'garmi' feeling after spicy or oily meals that seems to visit more often.
Impatience with everyone's pace: traffic, queues, colleagues, even your own family.

with_other_mizaj.damvi: A lively, warm match. Air (Damvi) brings an easy cheerfulness that softens your intensity, and your focus helps them finish what they start. You share heat, though, so arguments can ignite quickly. Agree on a cooling-off rule, keep serious talks for after meals, and let them run the social calendar while you run the plan.
with_other_mizaj.safravi: Two Fire spouses can build an empire or burn the kitchen down. You understand each other's ambition and pace, but nobody is naturally cooling the room. Take turns stepping back in arguments, divide responsibilities clearly so you are not competing, and schedule rest as seriously as you schedule work.
with_other_mizaj.balghami: Unani tradition sees this as a classic balance: the cool, moist calm of Water (Balghami) settles your fire, and your energy lifts their pace. You may find them slow; they may find you exhausting. Respect the difference. Let them take time to decide, and let yourself be cooled by their patience rather than irritated by it.
with_other_mizaj.saudavi: With Earth (Saudavi) you share dryness, so both of you can be precise, critical and serious. Their coolness tempers your heat, and their careful planning pairs well with your drive. The risk is a home that feels like an office. Make room for softness: compliments, shared meals and conversations that aren't about fixing anything.
